pos: n. pl. (deeds; things done, considered as weighed or judged)
etymology: Latin actio, a doing — the things a man does, considered together as the substance of his conduct.
biblical_def:
Talk no more so exceeding proudly; let not arrogancy come out of your mouth: for the LORD is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed.

Hannah's song does not merely say God sees actions; it says he weighs them, and a God of knowledge is precisely the reason the boastful mouth in the same verse has no ground to stand on. Weighed implies a standard, a scale, and an outcome, not a vague impression. The proud speech Hannah forbids is exposed as folly for one reason: the speaker imagines his actions are unmeasured, while the God of knowledge has already measured them exactly. Actions, in this single verse, becomes the whole ground of humility — a man talks proudly only where he forgets that everything he has done is already on the scale.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from ACTION: that which is done; a deed; an act; the exertion of power producing an effect, considered morally as subject to judgment.
webster_full: ACTION, n. The process of acting or doing; that which is done.
A deed; an act, considered as the effect of design or intention.
In a moral sense, conduct, considered as subject to the judgment of a rule or standard.
ACTIONS, n. pl. Deeds collectively; the sum of a person's conduct.
In Scripture, actions are weighed by God, who alone possesses perfect knowledge to judge them.
scriptures: Talk no more so exceeding proudly; let not arrogancy come out of your mouth: for the LORD is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed.

If thou sayest, Behold, we knew it not; doth not he that pondereth the heart consider it? and he that keepeth thy soul, doth not he know it? and shall not he render to every man according to his works?
corruption_summary: A therapeutic culture judges actions chiefly by intention and self-perception — I meant well, I felt it was right — quietly replacing Hannah's scale, held by a God of knowledge, with a scale each man is left to hold for himself.
corruption_paragraphs: "By him actions are weighed" leaves no room for a private appeal to good intentions overriding the deed actually done. Modern moral reasoning increasingly asks only what the actor meant, not what the action, weighed, actually was.

Proverbs 24:12 closes the same door from another angle: the excuse "we knew it not" does not survive a God who pondereth the heart. Actions are weighed by knowledge, not narrated by the excuses attached to them afterward.
roots_summary: No single Hebrew headword; the field is taken (weighed, measured), the same root behind the handwriting on the wall in Daniel 5.
roots_lines: Actions in Hannah's song are weighed, not merely observed.
The weighing is done by a God of knowledge, ruling out ignorance as an excuse.
Proud speech is exposed as folly against a God who has already measured the deed.
Proverbs 24:12 extends the principle to hidden motive as well as open deed.
Neither verse allows a man's own account of his actions to be the final word.
usage: By him actions are weighed — the ground of Hannah's warning against proud speech.
He that pondereth the heart — the same weighing extended to motive.
Shall not he render to every man according to his works — the outcome the weighing produces.

pos: n. pl. (reasons offered in proof or defense of a cause)
etymology: Latin argumentum, proof, evidence — a reason advanced to establish or defend a position.
biblical_def:
I would order my cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments. Surely I would speak to the Almighty, and I desire to reason with God.

Job's arguments are not complaints thrown at heaven but a case prepared, ordered, and filled — the language of a man approaching a court, not a man merely venting grief. He desires to reason with God, to speak to the Almighty directly rather than settle for his friends' secondhand theology. What makes the verse remarkable is not the boldness of wanting arguments before God but the assumption underneath it: that God is the kind of God who can be reasoned with, who receives an ordered cause rather than punishing the very attempt to bring one. Job's arguments never arrive, in the sense he expected, but the God who finally answers him out of the whirlwind does exactly what Job asked — he reasons with him, at length, to the end.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from ARGUMENT: a reason offered in proof; a fact or statement used to establish or overthrow a proposition.
webster_full: ARGUMENT, n. A reason offered for or against a proposition, opinion, or measure.
A process of reasoning; a course of reasoning to establish a position.
ARGUMENTS, n. pl. Reasons collectively arranged to support a cause.
Applied to Job's desire to order his cause and reason directly with God.
Distinguished from mere complaint by its structure: reasons prepared, not grief merely voiced.
scriptures: Job 23:4
I would order my cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments.
Job 13:3
Surely I would speak to the Almighty, and I desire to reason with God.
corruption_summary: A quietist piety that treats all questioning of providence as impertinent has little room for Job's arguments, forgetting that Scripture itself records God answering Job at length rather than silencing his desire to reason.
corruption_paragraphs: Some devotional cultures treat any ordered arguments brought before God as insufficiently submissive, preferring silence to Job's desire to reason with God. But Job's arguments were never a demand to overrule God; they were the honest labor of a man who believed God was reasonable enough to be reasoned with.

The whirlwind speeches that follow do not rebuke Job for wanting arguments; they answer with arguments of God's own, vastly larger than Job's, but arguments still. The pattern honors the reasoning mind even as it humbles it.
roots_summary: From tokachath (Heb.), reproofs or arguments, the word Job uses of the case he wishes to fill his mouth with.
roots_lines: Arguments in Job describes an ordered cause, not a raw complaint.
Job desires to reason with God directly, not merely with his friends.
Filling the mouth with arguments assumes God can be reasoned with.
The whirlwind speeches answer Job's desire, though not his expectation.
Scripture nowhere rebukes Job simply for wanting to reason with God.
usage: Fill my mouth with arguments — a case prepared, not a complaint vented.
I desire to reason with God — the honest labor behind Job's arguments.
God's own answer out of the whirlwind honors, while surpassing, Job's request.

pos: part. adj. (habituated; made familiar by repeated practice)
etymology: Old French acostumer, from Latin consuetudo, custom — worn into habit by repetition.
biblical_def:
Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil.

Jeremiah's accustomed is the hardest word in the verse. The Ethiopian's skin and the leopard's spots are not moral failures; they are simply what those creatures are. By placing accustomed to do evil in the same sentence, Jeremiah names something worse than an occasional sin — a settled, natural pattern, worn in by repetition until it functions like an unchangeable feature rather than a choice made fresh each day. The question is rhetorical and devastating: can ye also do good is not really a question at all, but a diagnosis. Habit has hardened into something the sinner experiences as identity, and only a power outside the sinner — never mere resolve — can answer a verse this bleak.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from ACCUSTOM: to make familiar by use; to habituate; to form a habit by repetition, until the practice becomes natural or fixed.
webster_full: ACCUSTOM, v.t. To make familiar by use; to habituate.
ACCUSTOMED, pp. Habituated; being in the habit of; used to.
Applied to a settled practice so repeated that it appears natural or fixed, like a physical trait.
In Jeremiah, used of moral habituation to evil so complete it is likened to an unalterable feature.
The word assumes that repetition can harden practice into something resembling nature, without excusing it as nature.
scriptures: Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil.
I spake unto thee in thy prosperity; but thou saidst, I will not hear. This hath been thy manner from thy youth, that thou obeyedst not my voice.
corruption_summary: Modern habit-formation language treats being accustomed to a sin as merely a pattern to optimize away with better systems, quietly dropping Jeremiah's point that some habituation is so deep it functions as bondage, answerable only to grace.
corruption_paragraphs: Self-improvement culture is confident that any accustomed pattern can be reprogrammed with enough discipline and the right habit-tracker. Jeremiah 13:23 is offered as the counter-case Scripture itself supplies: a habituation so total that the sinner needs a new nature, not merely a new routine.

Jeremiah 22:21 supplies the history behind the diagnosis — this hath been thy manner from thy youth. Accustomed sin is not usually sudden; it is cultivated across a lifetime of small refusals to hear, and it is answered only by the same grace that changes a nature, not merely a habit.
roots_summary: No single Hebrew headword; the force is carried by the whole proverb of the Ethiopian and the leopard, applied directly to habituated sin.
roots_lines: Accustomed names a habit worn in until it functions like nature.
Jeremiah's proverb compares it to an unchangeable physical trait.
The question can ye do good is rhetorical, not genuinely open.
This hath been thy manner from thy youth supplies the history of the habituation.
Only a changed nature, not mere resolve, answers a habituation this deep.
usage: Accustomed to do evil — habituation likened to an unchangeable trait.
This hath been thy manner from thy youth — the lifelong history behind the habit.
The proverb of skin and spots is Jeremiah's own diagnosis of settled sin.

pos: adv. (openly, plainly, in manifest form; not by riddle or figure)
etymology: Latin apparere, to appear, become visible — done in plain, visible manner, without concealment.
biblical_def:
With him will I speak mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches; and the similitude of the LORD shall he behold: wherefore then were ye not afraid to speak against my servant Moses? The LORD spake unto Moses face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend.

Apparently, in Numbers 12:8, is God's own description of the unique access he gave Moses, set directly against dark speeches — the visions, dreams, and riddles by which he ordinarily spoke to prophets. Moses alone received mouth to mouth, apparently, plain and open rather than veiled. Exodus 33:11 supplies the tenderness inside the formality: face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend. The rebuke to Aaron and Miriam that follows is severe precisely because they had compared their own access to Moses's, when Moses's apparently was categorically, not merely by degree, greater than anything given to another prophet before Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from APPARENT: open to view; visible; plain, evident, manifest, not hidden or disguised.
webster_full: APPARENT, a. Open to view; visible to the eye.
Plain; evident; indubitable, manifest to the understanding.
APPARENTLY, adv. Openly; evidently; in plain and manifest manner.
Contrasted in Scripture with dark speeches, visions, or dreams, as the mode of God's rarest revelation.
Used uniquely of the LORD's speech to Moses, unlike his ordinary manner with other prophets.
scriptures: Num 12:8
With him will I speak mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches; and the similitude of the LORD shall he behold: wherefore then were ye not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?

And the LORD spake unto Moses face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend. And he turned again into the camp: but his servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man, departed not out of the tabernacle.
corruption_summary: Modern usage has drained apparently of its force, using it now chiefly to hedge a claim the speaker doubts, the exact opposite of the certainty God attaches to the word in Numbers 12:8.
corruption_paragraphs: "Apparently" today usually signals uncertainty — apparently he left, meaning the speaker is not sure. God's apparently in Numbers 12 means the reverse: plain, certain, unmistakable, in contrast to dark speeches that require interpretation.

The distance between the two uses is worth marking, because it protects Moses's unique office from being flattened into ordinary prophetic experience — a mistake Aaron and Miriam made and were judged for making.
roots_summary: From mareh (Heb.), appearance or sight, paired with lo be-chidoth, not in riddles — the phrase God uses of Moses alone.
roots_lines: Apparently in Numbers 12:8 means plain and open, not uncertain.
It stands opposed to dark speeches, the ordinary mode of prophetic revelation.
Exodus 33:11 supplies the relational warmth behind the formal term.
Aaron and Miriam are rebuked for comparing their access to Moses's apparently.
The word marks Moses's office as unique among the prophets before Christ.
usage: Mouth to mouth, even apparently — God's own description of plain, unmediated speech.
Not in dark speeches — the contrast that defines apparently by what it excludes.
Face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend — the warmth behind the formal term.

pos: v. (past tense of bloom; put forth blossoms)
etymology: Middle English blome, blossom — to put forth flowers, the visible sign of living growth.
biblical_def:
And it came to pass, that on the morrow Moses went into the tabernacle of witness; and, behold, the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi was budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds. And it shall come to pass, that the man's rod, whom I shall choose, shall blossom: and I will make to cease from me the murmurings of the children of Israel.

Aaron's rod bloomed overnight, a dead stick doing in one night what a living almond tree needs a season to do — budded, brought forth buds, bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds, all four stages named in a single verse to remove any doubt that this was ordinary growth. God had promised exactly this sign in advance, tied explicitly to ending the murmurings against Aaron's priesthood. The rod that bloomed settled by unmistakable, undeniable life what argument could not settle: God himself had chosen the house of Levi, and a dead stick bearing fruit was his chosen way of silencing a rebellion no speech could end.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from BLOOM: to blossom; to flower; to produce blossoms, as the first sign of fruit-bearing.
webster_full: BLOOM, n. A blossom; the flower of a plant.
BLOOM, v.i. To produce or yield blossoms; to flower.
BLOOMED, pret. Put forth blossoms; flowered.
Used figuratively of a flourishing or thriving condition, as of youth or prosperity.
In Numbers, applied to Aaron's rod as the appointed sign ending the people's murmuring.
scriptures: Num 17:8

And it came to pass, that on the morrow Moses went into the tabernacle of witness; and, behold, the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi was budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds.
Num 17:5
And it shall come to pass, that the man's rod, whom I shall choose, shall blossom: and I will make to cease from me the murmurings of the children of Israel, whereby they murmur against you.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Bloomed survives chiefly as a plain narrative word tied to one of the Old Testament's clearest confirming signs.

The principle to recover is the pattern itself: God settled a leadership dispute not with more argument but with unmistakable, God-given fruit. Every claim to authority in the church still answers, ultimately, to whether it bears real fruit or merely asserts itself.
roots_summary: From tsits (Heb.), a blossom or flower, the same word used of the priestly plate and here of Aaron's rod.
roots_lines: Bloomed marks the third of four stages named in one verse.
A dead rod producing all four stages overnight rules out natural explanation.
The sign was promised in advance, tied to ending a specific rebellion.
God settled a leadership dispute with fruit, not with further argument.
The rod was kept afterward as a perpetual token against further murmuring.
usage: Budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds — four stages in one impossible night.
The man's rod, whom I shall choose, shall blossom — the sign promised before it was given.
Make to cease from me the murmurings — the sign's stated purpose.

pos: v. (past tense of blindfold; covered the eyes to prevent sight)
etymology: From blind + fold, to cover the eyes by folding a cloth over them — to deprive of sight by covering.
biblical_def:
And when they had blindfolded him, they struck him on the face, and asked him, saying, Prophesy, who is it that smote thee?

The men who blindfolded Christ did so to mock, not merely to strike him: the whole point of the game was to make him guess, by a power he supposedly claimed, who had struck him while he could not see. Every detail is calculated contempt, aimed at the specific claim that he was a prophet. That the eternal Word, who upholds all things and needs no eyes to see anything, submitted to being blindfolded by the hands he had made is one of the sharpest single images of the humiliation of the incarnate Son — power infinite, and treatment as a blind man's game.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from BLINDFOLD: to cover the eyes, so as to hinder seeing; to blind by covering.
webster_full: BLINDFOLD, v.t. To cover the eyes, so as to prevent seeing.
BLINDFOLDED, pp. Having the eyes covered; deprived of sight by a covering.
Used in Luke's Gospel of the mockery inflicted on Christ before his crucifixion.
The mockery consisted in demanding prophecy from one deliberately deprived of sight.
A deliberate insult aimed at Christ's claim to be a prophet, turned into a cruel game.
scriptures: And when they had blindfolded him, they struck him on the face, and asked him, saying, Prophesy, who is it that smote thee?
Isa 53:3
He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Blindfolded remains a plain narrative word tied to a single, deliberately shameful moment in the Passion.

The principle worth recovering is Isaiah's own preparation for it centuries earlier: we hid as it were our faces from him. The blindfold placed on Christ's face pictures, almost too literally, the world's own refusal to look at him rightly.
roots_summary: No single Greek headword of note; the significance lies entirely in the deliberate mockery the act was designed to inflict.
roots_lines: Blindfolded marks a moment of calculated mockery, not accidental cruelty.
The game demanded prophecy from one deprived, by their own hands, of sight.
The insult targeted Christ's specific claim to be a prophet.
Isaiah 53:3 anticipates the world hiding its own face from him centuries before.
The Word who sees all things submitted to being denied sight by his own creatures.
usage: When they had blindfolded him, they struck him on the face — mockery structured as a cruel game.
Prophesy, who is it that smote thee — the specific insult behind the blindfold.
We hid as it were our faces from him — Isaiah's earlier picture of the same rejection.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon blaecra, comparative of blaec, black — of a darker hue, used figuratively of famine, grief, or ruin.
biblical_def:
Their visage is blacker than a coal; they are not known in the streets: their skin cleaveth to their bones; it is withered, it is become like a stick.

Lamentations sets blacker directly against the earlier description of the same people's former glory, purer than snow, whiter than milk. The contrast is the whole force of the verse: famine and siege have so wasted the survivors of Jerusalem that they are unrecognizable, their visage blacker than a coal, their skin withered onto their bones. This is judgment made visible on the body — not a metaphor for suffering but an eyewitness report of what covenant unfaithfulness, run to its end, actually looks like on human faces once admired in the streets and now not known there at all.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from BLACK: destitute of light; of the darkest color; comparative degree, darker still, often figuratively of calamity or mourning.
webster_full: BLACK, a. Destitute of light; of the color of soot or coal; dark.
Figuratively, dismal, mournful, calamitous.
BLACKER, a. Comparative of Black; darker; more thoroughly destitute of light or color.
Applied in Lamentations to faces wasted by famine, siege, and grief.
Set deliberately against a former state of ruddy health, to measure the extent of the fall.
scriptures: Lam 4:8
Their visage is blacker than a coal; they are not known in the streets: their skin cleaveth to their bones; it is withered, it is become like a stick.
Lam 4:7
Her Nazarites were purer than snow, they were whiter than milk, they were more ruddy in body than rubies, their polishing was of sapphire:
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Blacker in Lamentations is a plain report of famine's effect on the body, not a term the age has repurposed.

The principle to recover is the deliberate before-and-after Lamentations sets up: covenant unfaithfulness is not merely a private spiritual matter but has visible, physical, communal consequences, and the prophet refuses to look away from either the glory or the ruin.
roots_summary: From chashak (Heb.), to be dark or black, used here of famine's visible ruin upon once-honored men.
roots_lines: Blacker is set deliberately against the former glory named one verse earlier.
The change is physical and visible, not merely emotional.
Skin cleaveth to their bones names starvation plainly, without euphemism.
Not known in the streets shows how total the change was.
Lamentations records judgment's visible cost without looking away.
usage: Blacker than a coal — famine's visible mark on once-honored faces.
Not known in the streets — the extent of the change measured by recognition lost.
Set against purer than snow, whiter than milk one verse earlier — glory and ruin side by side.

pos: v. (the cry of a watchdog; here, negated — a failure to warn)
etymology: Anglo-Saxon beorcan, to bark — the natural warning cry of a dog set to guard.
biblical_def:
His watchmen are blind: they are all ignorant, they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark; sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber.

A dog kept for one purpose, to bark when danger comes, that cannot bark is worse than no dog at all — it gives the appearance of protection while providing none. Isaiah's watchmen are named dumb dogs on exactly this ground: their whole office was to warn, and they cannot bark, sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber while the flock they were set to guard is exposed. The indictment is aimed squarely at leaders who possess the position of watchman without the function of one, and the specific detail that they love to slumber removes any excuse of accident — this is a chosen, preferred negligence, not an occasional lapse.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from BARK: the noise made by a dog; to utter the sharp, abrupt cry natural to a dog, especially in warning or defense.
webster_full: BARK, n. The noise made by a dog.
BARK, v.i. To utter the sharp cry natural to a dog, especially as a warning of danger.
Figuratively, to clamor, or to give warning as by an outcry.
Applied negatively in Isaiah of watchmen who fail entirely at their one appointed function.
A dog that cannot bark is worse than useless for the purpose it was kept.
scriptures: His watchmen are blind: they are all ignorant, they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark; sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber.
corruption_summary: Modern church leadership sometimes prizes an agreeable, uncritical presence over the plain duty to warn, quietly rewarding exactly the dumb dogs Isaiah condemns because a watchman who cannot bark never disturbs anyone's rest.
corruption_paragraphs: A pastor or leader praised chiefly for being pleasant, never sounding an alarm over false doctrine or open sin, fits Isaiah's dumb dogs precisely — not from ignorance of danger, necessarily, but from loving to slumber more than loving the flock.

The remedy is not harshness for its own sake but simple faithfulness to the one function the office exists for: watchmen are kept to bark, and a congregation that has trained its watchmen into silence has trained itself into exactly the exposure Isaiah describes.
roots_summary: From tsapah (Heb.), to watch or look out, the office named directly before the indictment that these particular watchmen cannot perform it.
roots_lines: Bark names the one function a watch-dog exists to perform.
Cannot bark is worse than not being a dog at all — false security is manufactured.
Blind, ignorant, and loving to slumber are named as the causes, not excuses.
The indictment targets office without function, not merely incompetence.
Isaiah aims this squarely at Israel's own appointed leaders.
usage: Dumb dogs, they cannot bark — office held without its one required function.
Loving to slumber — chosen negligence, not accidental lapse.
His watchmen are blind — the root cause named before the failure itself.

pos: v. (to help; to give aid, especially in business or need)
etymology: Latin assistere, to stand by — to stand beside another in order to help, aid, or support.
biblical_def:
I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea. That ye receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints, and that ye assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you: for she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also.

Assist, in Paul's commendation of Phebe, is a debt owed, not a favor granted. He commends her as a servant of the church and a succourer of many, including himself, and then instructs Rome to assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of — practical, specific help for a woman whose own record of help to others is already established. The word sits inside ordinary church business: hospitality, travel, provision, the unglamorous logistics that let ministry actually happen. Paul does not ask Rome to admire Phebe; he asks them to assist her, matching in kind the succour she had already given.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from ASSIST: to help; to aid; to succor; to give support in some undertaking or need.
webster_full: ASSIST, v.t. To help; to aid; to succor.
To stand by another in order to further his design, or to give strength or support.
ASSISTANCE, n. Help; aid; furtherance.
Used in Romans of practical aid owed to a fellow servant of the church.
Distinguished from mere admiration by requiring an actual, specific act of help.
scriptures: Rom 16:2
That ye receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints, and that ye assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you: for she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also.
Rom 16:1
I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea:
corruption_summary: Church life sometimes reduces assist to a vague spiritual sentiment — prayers and good wishes — while quietly declining the specific, practical help Paul actually asked Rome to give Phebe in whatsoever business she hath need.
corruption_paragraphs: It costs little to say a kind word about a faithful servant of the church; it costs something to assist her in whatsoever business she hath need, which is exactly the concrete standard Paul sets and Rome is commanded to meet.

Phebe's own record, a succourer of many, and of myself also, is presented as the reason the assistance is owed, not a suggestion. The pattern reverses the usual order: honor a proven servant by matching her help, not merely by praising it.
roots_summary: No single Greek headword beyond paristemi, to stand by or furnish — the ordinary word for practical help extended to a named, commended servant.
roots_lines: Assist is commanded specifically, not merely encouraged in general.
Phebe's own prior succour is the stated ground for the assistance owed her.
Whatsoever business she hath need of you leaves the form of help open but the obligation fixed.
Paul includes himself among those Phebe had already succoured.
The word belongs to the ordinary, practical logistics of church life.
usage: Assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you — a specific, practical obligation.
A servant of the church... a succourer of many — Phebe's own record, cited as grounds.
Receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints — hospitality paired with practical assistance.

pos: v. (past tense of belie; spoken falsely of, misrepresented, denied against truth)
etymology: Anglo-Saxon beleogan, be- + leogan, to lie — to speak falsely concerning a person or thing, misrepresenting the truth about it.
biblical_def:
They have belied the LORD, and said, It is not he; neither shall evil come upon us; neither shall we see sword nor famine.

To belie the LORD is not merely to disbelieve him but to misrepresent him actively, putting false words in the place of true ones: it is not he, neither shall evil come upon us. Jeremiah's charge is precise — the people did not simply doubt God's warnings, they constructed a counter-claim about his character and intentions and asserted it as though it were his own word. Belied names this particular sin: not silence toward God, but false testimony about him, spoken with enough confidence that a hearer might mistake it for theology. The sword and famine that follow answer the lie with the very reality it had denied.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from BELIE: to give the lie to; to speak falsely of; to represent falsely, so as to convey an untrue impression.
webster_full: BELIE, v.t. To give the lie to; to show to be false.
To speak falsely of; to tell lies concerning; to slander by false representation.
BELIED, pp. Represented falsely; falsely charged or described.
Applied in Jeremiah to false claims made about the character and intentions of the LORD himself.
Distinguished from unbelief by involving active, false assertion, not merely doubt.
scriptures: Jer 5:12
They have belied the LORD, and said, It is not he; neither shall evil come upon us; neither shall we see sword nor famine:
corruption_summary: A therapeutic reinterpretation of God, confident that judgment, wrath, and holiness are not really him, repeats Jeremiah's exact charge in modern dress: belying the LORD by asserting a more comfortable version of him in place of the true one.
corruption_paragraphs: "It is not he" is the pattern behind every soft gospel that promises neither evil, nor sword, nor famine will ever come, regardless of covenant unfaithfulness. The sin named belied is precisely this: substituting a preferred account of God for the true one and preaching it with confidence.
Jeremiah does not treat this as an innocent theological error. It is named alongside sword and famine as the specific lie the true God's real actions would answer, and answer it plainly did.
roots_summary: From kachash (Heb.), to lie, deny, or deal falsely, used here of a false claim made directly about the LORD's own character and intentions.
roots_lines: Belied names active false testimony, not mere doubt.
The false claim concerns God's own character and future action.
It is not he is the specific lie Jeremiah records and refutes.
The judgment that follows answers the lie point for point.
The sin is theological confidence in a falsehood, not honest uncertainty.
usage: They have belied the LORD — false testimony about God's own character.
It is not he — the specific denial that constitutes the lie.
Neither shall evil come upon us — the false comfort the lie was built to provide.
